newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerians vote peacefully in test-case election.
newsitem.headline: Nigerians vote peacefully in test-case election.

text.p: Nigerians voted peacefully on Saturday in local elections seen as a test of the military's commitment to return the populous African nation to democracy.

Authorities ordered all transport off the roads for the polling period from 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) to 4 p.m (1500 GMT) to ensure people went to polling stations, which are supposed to be within walking distance for all voters.
Shops and businesses closed across the country. In a district of the largest city Lagos, soldiers horse-whipped and frog-marched a group of people found trading, witnesses said.
Police in full riot gear patrolled or stood in personnel carriers at strategic positions but away from polling centres.
There were no immediate reports of serious incidents in Lagos or the outlying southwestern region, the bastion of opposition to military rule and the army's civil rule programme.
"People are voting peacefully here. No one has caused any trouble," said a spokesman for the police command in Abeokuta, the hometown of jailed presidential claimant Moshood Abiola.

The last time Nigerians voted to end the army's long stranglehold on power ended in fiasco. The military abruptly scrapped the June 1993 presidential poll as Abiola, a wealthy businessman was coasting to victory.
Abacha seized power in the confusion that ensued, but Nigeria plunged further into crisis after Abiola was detained in June 1994 for proclaiming himself president.
The army has ruled Nigeria for most of the time since independence from Britain in 1960. There has been widespread skepticism about the military's promise to step down in 1998.

Speculation is rife that Abacha will not hand over power to a civilian president, unless he is the civilian. Abacha insists the army will keep its promise to return to barracks, but has so far avoided addressing the burning issue of his own future.
Pro-democracy groups, who denounce the military's democracy programme as a sham, urged people to ignore local elections held as a test run exactly a year ago on non-party basis.
This time they have not urged a boycott but neither have they shown any enthusiasm for the ballot.
The poll to elect chairmen and councillors to more than 770 town halls is the first multi-party ballot since 1993.

Voting started off on time but slowly in Lagos, with only a trickle of voters noticeable at most polling stations. Officials said this was because there were many more polling stations this time than in last year's non-party elections.
Enthusiasm was markedly higher in poorer neighbourhoods.

Polling in the capital Abuja started on schedule but rowdy scenes erupted at some polling stations where voters complained their names were missing from voter lists or that numbers on their cards did not match those on the register.
"I was registered here as voter number two but now my name is not on the list. I must vote," said voter John Dare at the NYSC polling station in the capital's Area 2.
Residents reported heavy turnout in Bauchi state in northern Nigeria, where support for the transition programme is strong. Abacha, like most of Nigeria's rulers, is from the north.
No established international or Western monitoring groups were invited to observe the elections although a 38-member U.S. team of mostly African Americans arrived this week.
The government has been shunned by Western powers since the 1995 hanging of writer Ken Saro Wiwa and eight other minority activists after a special court convicted them of murder.
The National Electoral Commission of Nigeria (NECON) released final figures showing nearly 56 million voters had been registered for the poll from a population of about 100 million.
